questions.question: What is a code review and why do software teams do it?
questions.title: What Is a Code Review and Why Teams Do It
questions.direct_answer: A code review is the process of a peer examining your code changes before they are merged, catching bugs, enforcing standards, and spreading knowledge across the team.

interviewer_intent.testing: Team collaboration awareness — software development is a team sport
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating code review as optional quality gatekeeping rather than a core collaborative practice
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that code reviews also transfer knowledge — the reviewer learns about the codebase too

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A code review is when one or more teammates examine the code changes you're about to merge into the shared codebase. Teams do this for several reasons. First, bug detection: a second pair of eyes catches logical errors, edge cases, and security issues that the author missed. Second, code quality: reviewers check for readability, naming, structure, and adherence to team conventions. Third, knowledge sharing: when I review someone's code, I learn about that part of the system. When they review mine, they learn about my changes. Over time, the team has collective understanding of the whole codebase rather than knowledge silos. Fourth, mentoring: code review is one of the best ways for seniors to guide juniors — specific, in-context feedback on real code is more effective than abstract advice.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Code review: peer examination of changes before merging
Bug detection: second set of eyes catches what the author missed
Code quality: enforce conventions, readability, and architecture standards
Knowledge sharing: reviewer and author both learn from the process
Mentoring: seniors guide juniors through specific, in-context feedback

questions.question: What do reviewers typically look for during a Java code review?
questions.title: What Reviewers Look For in a Java Code Review
questions.direct_answer: Reviewers check for correctness (does it work and handle edge cases), readability (is it clear), security (no vulnerabilities), performance (no obvious bottlenecks), and test coverage.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of professional code standards — freshers should know what to look for in their own code before submitting
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only mentioning 'does it work' — missing readability, security, and tests
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that a good reviewer asks 'would I understand this code six months from now?' as a readability test

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When I review Java code, I look at several dimensions. First is correctness: does the code actually do what it's supposed to? Does it handle null inputs, empty collections, boundary values? Second is readability: can I understand this code in 30 seconds? Are variable names meaningful? Are methods short and focused on one thing? Third is security: are there SQL injection risks? Are sensitive values like passwords getting logged? Is input validated? Fourth is performance: are there N+1 query problems? Are we creating objects we don't need? Fifth is tests: does the PR include tests for the new behavior? Are edge cases covered? I also check for adherence to team conventions — naming patterns, exception handling style, logging patterns.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Correctness: handles edge cases, null inputs, boundary conditions
Readability: clear naming, single-responsibility methods, no unnecessary complexity
Security: no SQL injection, no logging sensitive data, input validation
Performance: no N+1 queries, appropriate data structures
Tests: new behavior is tested, edge cases covered, tests are readable

questions.question: How do you give effective and constructive code review feedback?
questions.title: How to Give Good Code Review Feedback
questions.direct_answer: Good code review feedback is specific about what to change and why, suggests an alternative rather than just criticizing, distinguishes blocking issues from preferences, and is never personal.

interviewer_intent.testing: Team collaboration and communication skills — code review is as much about communication as it is about code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving vague feedback like 'this is bad' or 'rewrite this' without explaining why or suggesting an alternative
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use the concept of 'nit:' prefix for minor style preferences — signals that the comment won't block the merge

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Code review feedback should be something the author can actually act on. Vague comments like 'this doesn't look right' are frustrating. Effective feedback is specific: it points to the exact line or block, explains the concern clearly, and ideally suggests an alternative. It's also important to distinguish between blocking issues and preferences. If there's a bug or a security issue, that's a must-fix. If it's a naming style or a minor refactor, I use a prefix like 'nit:' to signal it's a suggestion, not a requirement. And feedback should never be personal — I'm commenting on the code, not the person. I also try to acknowledge good code. If I see a particularly elegant solution, saying so reinforces good habits and makes the review feel balanced.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Be specific: point to exact line, explain the issue, suggest an alternative
Distinguish blocking from preferences: use 'nit:' for optional style suggestions
Never personal: comment on the code, not the person
Explain the why: 'this could cause a NullPointerException because...'
Acknowledge good solutions — positive feedback reinforces good habits

questions.question: How should you respond to code review feedback as a junior developer?
questions.title: How to Receive Code Review Feedback as a Junior Developer
questions.direct_answer: Treat feedback as an opportunity to learn, not a personal attack — thank reviewers for good catches, ask clarifying questions when you don't understand the reasoning, and don't argue about style preferences.

interviewer_intent.testing: Coachability and team fit — a junior who reacts defensively to feedback is hard to work with
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Getting defensive or treating all feedback as correct without thinking critically
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that it's okay to respectfully disagree with a suggestion and explain your reasoning — code review is a dialogue

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: My default is to treat code review feedback as a gift — someone took time to read my code carefully and help me improve it. When I get a comment pointing out a bug I missed, my first reaction is genuine appreciation, not defensiveness. I try to understand the reviewer's concern before deciding how to respond. If the feedback makes sense, I fix it and mark the comment as resolved. If I don't understand why something is a problem, I ask a clarifying question: 'Could you explain why this approach would cause issues?' If I genuinely disagree, I explain my thinking clearly and respectfully. Code review is a conversation, not a decree. One thing I avoid is taking style preferences personally. If a senior developer prefers a different pattern, even if mine is technically correct, I generally defer unless I have a strong reason.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Default to appreciation — reviewer invested time to help you improve
Understand before responding — ask why if the reason isn't clear
It's okay to disagree — but explain your reasoning respectfully
Defer on style preferences unless you have a strong technical reason
Code review is a dialogue, not a lecture — both parties can learn

questions.question: What is a good size for a pull request and why does it matter?
questions.title: Pull Request Size Best Practices
questions.direct_answer: A good pull request is small and focused on a single concern — ideally under 400 lines — because large PRs are hard to review thoroughly and sit open longer, delaying feedback and increasing merge conflicts.

interviewer_intent.testing: Team collaboration mindset — candidates who create huge PRs show poor collaboration habits
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking bigger PRs mean more output — in practice they slow down delivery and create poor-quality reviews
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the concept of feature flags for enabling large features incrementally, allowing small PRs even for large features

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: There's a saying in software teams: a PR with 10 lines gets 10 comments; a PR with 500 lines gets approved with a 'LGTM' emoji. When a PR is very large, reviewers can't give it the attention it deserves — they get overwhelmed, miss things, or just approve to unblock the author. Small, focused PRs — ideally changing one thing — are much easier to review thoroughly. Small PRs also stay open for less time. A 50-line PR might be reviewed in an hour; a 1000-line PR might sit for days, blocking the author and accumulating merge conflicts. In practice, I aim for PRs that address one concern: one feature, one bug fix, one refactor. If a feature requires many changes, I break it into a sequence of smaller PRs. For very large features, feature flags let me merge code that's not yet active for users, allowing small incremental PRs without exposing an incomplete feature.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Target under 400 lines changed per PR — reviewers cannot thoroughly review huge diffs
One concern per PR: one bug fix, one feature, one refactor
Large PRs sit open longer, accumulate merge conflicts, and get rubber-stamp reviews
Break large features into sequences of small PRs
Feature flags: merge code without activating it — enables small PRs for large features

questions.question: What is the difference between a code review and pair programming?
questions.title: Code Review vs Pair Programming
questions.direct_answer: Code review is an asynchronous post-coding inspection, while pair programming is real-time collaborative coding where two developers work together simultaneously.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of team collaboration practices and quality assurance methods
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking they are interchangeable or that one replaces the other
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention when each is most effective and that mature teams often use both

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Code review and pair programming are both collaborative quality practices, but they work very differently in terms of timing and format.

Code review is asynchronous. A developer finishes writing code, opens a pull request, and then one or more teammates review that code — reading through it, leaving comments, suggesting improvements, and ultimately approving or requesting changes. This happens after the code is already written. It's great for catching logic issues, enforcing style standards, sharing knowledge across the team, and maintaining a reviewable audit trail. Tools like GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket all have built-in code review workflows.

Pair programming, on the other hand, is real-time. Two developers sit together — physically or virtually — and write code together simultaneously. One person is the 'driver' typing the code, and the other is the 'navigator' thinking about the bigger picture, catching mistakes as they happen, and guiding direction. Roles can swap regularly. Because you have two sets of eyes on the code as it's being written, many bugs and design issues are caught before they even get committed.

Both approaches have value. Code review scales well because reviewers can review multiple PRs asynchronously, but feedback comes late. Pair programming is more intensive and expensive in time, but it produces higher quality code upfront and is excellent for knowledge transfer — especially useful when onboarding new team members.

As a fresher joining a team, you'll almost certainly encounter code reviews. Pair programming might be used occasionally, particularly when working on complex features or learning a new system.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Code review is asynchronous — happens after code is written via pull requests
Pair programming is synchronous — two developers code together in real time
Code review scales well; pair programming is higher-intensity but catches issues earlier
Both can be used together — they are complementary, not competing practices

questions.question: What are common things you should check for when reviewing someone else's code?
questions.title: What to Check in a Code Review
questions.direct_answer: During a code review, check for correctness, readability, error handling, code duplication, security issues, and adherence to team coding standards.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands software quality beyond just making code work
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only mentioning syntax or formatting and missing deeper concerns like correctness and security
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that the goal is constructive feedback, not finding fault — code reviews are a learning tool

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A thorough code review goes beyond checking if the code compiles. There are several layers I'd look at.

First, correctness — does the code actually do what it's supposed to do? Does it handle edge cases, like null inputs, empty collections, or unexpected values? This is the most important check because the code might look clean but still have logic bugs.

Second, readability — is the code easy to understand? Are variable and method names meaningful? Is the code structured in a way that another developer could quickly grasp what it does without needing a long explanation?

Third, error handling — does the code handle exceptions properly? Are there try-catch blocks where needed? Are exceptions logged and not silently swallowed?

Fourth, code duplication — is the developer repeating logic that already exists elsewhere in the codebase? If yes, can it be extracted into a shared utility method?

Fifth, security basics — especially for web applications, are things like user input being validated? Are there obvious SQL injection or XSS vulnerabilities?

Sixth, coding standards — does the code follow the team's established patterns, naming conventions, and style guide?

Finally, I'd also consider performance for any loops or database queries that could be slow at scale.

As a fresher, I might not catch every issue, but having this checklist mindset shows I take code quality seriously. The goal of code review is improvement and shared learning, not just finding fault.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Check correctness first — does the code handle edge cases and do what's intended?
Review readability — clear naming, logical structure, and understandable flow
Verify error handling — exceptions should be caught, logged, and not silently swallowed
Look for duplication, security concerns, and adherence to team coding standards

questions.question: Why is it important to write small, focused commits and pull requests?
questions.title: Small Commits and PRs
questions.direct_answer: Small, focused commits and pull requests are easier to review, easier to debug, and easier to revert if something goes wrong.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of professional development workflow habits
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking bigger commits are more productive because they get more done at once
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect small PRs to faster review cycles and lower risk of merge conflicts

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Writing small, focused commits and pull requests is a professional habit that makes teams much more effective, and it's something senior developers genuinely care about.

The first reason is reviewability. If a pull request changes 1,000 lines across 20 files touching different features, it becomes very difficult for a reviewer to understand the intent and catch bugs. A reviewer might spend an hour on a large PR and still miss issues. A small, focused PR with a clear purpose — like 'add input validation to the user registration endpoint' — can be reviewed quickly and thoroughly.

The second reason is debuggability. When something breaks in production, small commits let you pinpoint the exact commit that introduced the problem using tools like `git bisect`. If your commits are large and mix multiple concerns, isolating the cause of a bug is much harder.

The third reason is safer rollback. If a small, focused commit introduces a regression, it's trivial to revert just that one commit without undoing unrelated work. With a massive commit, reverting it means losing multiple unrelated changes.

The fourth reason is merge conflict reduction. Small PRs get merged quickly and don't sit open for long, reducing the chance that other developers' changes will conflict with yours.

As a fresher, developing the habit of committing logical, small units of work — one feature, one bug fix, one refactor — will make you a much easier developer to work with and will signal professionalism to your team.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Small PRs are faster to review and easier for reviewers to thoroughly understand
Small commits make it easier to find bugs using git bisect and similar tools
Focused commits are easier to revert without losing unrelated work
Smaller PRs reduce merge conflict risk by staying open for less time
